title: Is Nebius Stock a Buy After Its 36% Pullback?
detail:
Is Nebius Stock a Buy After Its 36% Pullback?
Justin Pope, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 1, 2026 at 1:35 PM CST 5 min read
NBIS
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The artificial intelligence (AI) trade has been the driving force behind the stock market's strong performance these past few years. But recent concerns over funding for data centers and other AI infrastructure have sparked a sell-off among AI stocks over the past month.

Nebius Group (NASDAQ: NBIS), an AI cloud company, has been caught in the turmoil. Shares traded near $250 in September, nearly touching $300 per share before the AI trade began to lose steam.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

All of a sudden, Nebius sits 36% off its high. Should investors buy Nebius Group stock? The financing concerns matter because Nebius needs substantial capital to build the AI data centers it leases to AI companies. Here's what you need to know.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
The growth is impressive and undeniable

Computing power is arguably the most important bottleneck for AI's advancement and adoption. Smarter AI models and more users both translate to higher demand for compute.

Nebius plays an important role in this. The company builds specialized data centers, fitted with Nvidia graphics processing unit (GPU) chips designed specifically for AI workloads. It then leases them to its customers, primarily Microsoft and Meta Platforms.

These two companies are among the largest AI hyperscalers, so their computing needs are setting Nebius on an explosive growth trajectory. Wall Street analysts estimate that revenue growth will continue to accelerate, finishing this year at around $3.34 billion and then soaring to $12.24 billion next year.

NBIS Revenue (TTM) data by YCharts.

Nebius has more than $40 billion in long-term commitments from investment-grade customers, and AI GPU leader Nvidia has a stake in the company. Nebius is also among the first companies to offer access to AI servers using Nvidia's Vera Rubin AI chip platform.

The financing is a legitimate cause for concern

A major issue facing Nebius is that it must build out its AI data centers before it can really monetize them. As a result, the company is burning through startling amounts of capital ahead of this expected revenue surge next year. Management anticipates $20 billion to $25 billion in capital expenditures (capex) this year and is funding them through a combination of debt and new stock.

All that growth has certainly enticed investors, who have driven Nebius' market capitalization to $43 billion. That's arguably a hefty valuation for a company that's basically diluting existing shareholders and loading up its balance sheet with debt before it's consistently profitable.

It's only fair to wonder what the future holds. The industry-wide concerns center on speculation about how much more capital is available in the debt markets for these companies to access as AI spending continues adding up.

Nebius has strong support from its critical customers

Elon Musk recently predicted on X that many AI cloud companies could fail, stating that debt markets have already pulled back on lending to companies without meaningful revenue streams outside of data centers. That said, Nebius may be on solid footing.

Nebius is receiving significant upfront payments from its customers as part of its deals. Management guided for total prepayments of around $9 billion in 2026, helping the company stomach its sky-high capex. Nebius also still had about $8 billion in cash at the end of the second quarter.

Is the stock a buy?

There's no clear-cut answer because it's difficult to know what Nebius' margins will ultimately look like. More profitable companies often sustain higher valuations than unprofitable or low-margin businesses.

There's also a risk that hyperscalers will eventually back off their aggressive spending if they cannot monetize AI enough to justify the continued spending.

As of right now, the stock trades at less than four times next year's revenue estimate of $12.24 billion. That's pretty low and may not require unrealistic profit margins to justify it, given the staggering anticipated revenue growth next year.

That makes Nebius a solid buy for risk-seeking growth investors.

The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO) has always been one of the best long-term investments for everyday, regular folks. But there are some legitimate questions about whether now is the right time to invest. Is it too top-heavy? Is it too concentrated in tech? Is it primed for a pullback given how far it's risen in the past few years?

Currently, it has roughly 40% of the index invested in tech stocks. Almost 40% is accounted for just by the top 10 holdings. Both are historically high figures, which makes the S&P 500 less diversified than at almost any other point in its history.

Despite this, I believe the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF remains one of the best long-term investment options. A big part of the reason why is the same reason it's become historically concentrated -- its market-cap weighting methodology.

That strategy helps the index evolve over time in line with the state of the U.S. economy. At different points in history, railroads, energy, financials, and now technology have been the biggest sector allocations. If something else emerges in the future, the index composition will likely change again to give that greater weighting. The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) essentially reconstitutes itself over time.

Plus, let's not forget that it includes hundreds of the biggest and most successful companies in the United States. That makes an ideal portfolio cornerstone in almost any situation. detail:
Why Netflix Stock Could Double From This Dip
John Ballard, The Motley Fool

Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX) stock hit a new 52-week low on Oct. 27, 2026, down 33% year to date. That's a steep fall for a leading entertainment brand that still grows revenue by double digits.

Still, a stock trading at a discount to the market while growing revenue by double digits is worth a closer look. Here's why Netflix is in a better competitive position than the stock's performance suggests, and why the sell-off could set up a double over the next five years.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Slowing U.S. growth explains the sell-off

Revenue growth has slowed for three straight quarters, from 18% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 12% in Q3 2026. The laggard is the U.S. market. During the third-quarter earnings call, Co-CEO Greg Peters said, "We know that we can do better, and that better is our upside."

Peters said management is focused on improving its U.S. content slate, which is expected to deliver better results. The streaming market is competitive, with YouTube continuing to dominate viewing time, according to Nielsen. Netflix is behind YouTube in the No. 2 spot, but that also means it's ahead of dozens of other streaming services, including Walt Disney, Roku, and Amazon Prime.

Netflix subscribers are staying, and every region is growing

Every region grew revenue by double digits year over year last quarter: 11% in the U.S. and Canada; 11% in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa; 17% in Latin America; and 12% in Asia-Pacific. In India, a strong slate of local hits lifted viewing hours 24% year over year.

Importantly, slowing U.S. growth doesn't mean subscribers are canceling. Peters said, "Q3 churn, both globally and in the United States, improved year on year," meaning fewer members canceled. And this is following recent price increases, including in the U.S. When people keep paying more without leaving, the service is delivering value.

Image source: Getty Images.

Netflix continues to grow and earn a healthy margin on revenue. It reported nearly $16 billion in trailing-12-month operating income on $50 billion of revenue, providing ample resources to fund a growing content budget and win more viewing time in the U.S. market.

Enough earnings growth to double the stock

Management reiterated its long-term financial goals to sustain double-digit revenue growth, increase profit margins, and grow free cash flow. If it delivers, earnings should grow faster than revenue, setting up a rebound in the stock.

The stock trades at about 17 times 2026 earnings estimates, as of Oct. 27, 2026 -- a slight discount to the S&P 500 average forward price-to-earnings multiple of 19. Analysts expect earnings to grow about 21% annually in the next several years. That growth can double earnings, and the stock, in the next five years, assuming it continues to trade at the same earnings multiple.

There's always been competition in entertainment, so I would look at execution on the content slate as the main risk. If Netflix can't land more hit shows at home, revenue growth could continue to slow, and the stock might continue to underperform. I wouldn't buy the stock expecting a quick rebound, but at this valuation, Netflix appears undervalued and set up to deliver excellent returns for patient investors.

detail:
Here's What $6,000 Invested in Micron Could Be Worth in 2028
Bram Berkowitz, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 1, 2026 at 12:20 PM CST 5 min read
MU
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Micron (NASDAQ: MU) has had a fantastic year, with the stock up over 200%.

The memory maker became the center of the next major bottleneck in artificial intelligence. As clusters of graphics processing units (GPUs) scaled to meet the needs of larger AI models, memory, which feeds data to the GPUs in various capacities, also came into high demand.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Memory prices soared, resulting in fantastic results for companies like Micron. Here's what $6,000 invested in the stock could be worth by 2029.

Image source: Getty Images.
Wall Street expects Micron's earnings to soar

Micron is one of the largest makers of NAND flash memory and dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), both of which play different roles in feeding data to GPUs.

NAND is cheaper and offers high-capacity storage useful for holding the massive data sets that feed GPUs during training.

DRAM is high-speed memory that holds data only while powered. In AI systems, stacks of DRAM silicon are used to create high bandwidth memory (HBM), which sits next to GPUs and holds model parameters during training and inference.

Due to the massive demand for AI and, therefore, GPUs and data, Micron COO Manish Bhatia said on the company's most recent earnings call that "we really don't have line of sight to when supply and demand balances."

Memory companies are often viewed as cyclical because it's difficult to match supply with demand, which can result in a supply glut at some point in the cycle. In this super-charged cycle, many investors have wondered if things will be different.

Micron has secured 16 Strategic Customer Agreements, with deals running three to five years, an atypical development for memory companies.

As a result of all this, Micron's earnings are projected to soar. Micron recently completed its fiscal year 2026 (ending Aug. 26), reporting diluted earnings per share of over $74. For fiscal year 2027, Wall Street consensus estimates project Micron's earnings to surge to over $172 per share, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence.

In fiscal 2029, the 10 Wall Street analysts who have submitted estimates to S&P Global expect Micron's earnings to exceed $212 per share. Valuing Micron on its current forward 12-month earnings of roughly $172, the stock trades at a 5.65x multiple.

If I simply carry that multiple forward, Micron should trade at $1,197 per share in 2028, based on its forward projected earnings for fiscal 2029. That implies roughly 23% upside, meaning a $6,000 investment would be worth $7,380.

Nvidia and Nike are among the latest companies to object to tokenized versions of their shares trading on the ICE-OKX venue, bringing the total to 50, according to Eleanor Terrett.

The venture had initially proposed tokenizing shares from 62 companies.

Objectors include Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan, and the venue's notice gives no reasons for their objections.

A planned venue for trading tokenized U.S. stocks from New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) and crypto exchange OKX has hit a wall, as Nvidia (NVDA) and Nike (NKE) joined a growing list of companies objecting to their shares being offered on it.

The number of companies objecting to OKXICE tokenizing their shares has grown to 50, journalist Eleanor Terrett said on X on Sunday. She said Nike, Costco (COST), Micron (MU), Reddit (RDDT) and Nvidia were among the new additions.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Source: @EleanorTerrett/x

The venture had initially proposed tokenizing shares from 62 companies, Terrett said.

Who's On The List

The venue's notice listed objectors including Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOGL), Goldman Sachs (GS), JPMorgan (JPM), Broadcom (AVGO), Verizon (VZ), Intel (INTC) and Walmart (WMT).

AI-linked companies like CoreWeave (CRWV), Oracle (ORCL) and Arm Holdings (ARM) were also on it, along with CrowdStrike (CRWD), Corning (GLW), IREN (IREN) and Bloom Energy (BE). The objections piled up quickly. The venue's October 19 notice showed 16 objectors.

How Would The Venue Work?

OKXICE is a 50-50 joint venture between ICE and OKX, and plans to run under a temporary exemption the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) issued in September, which lets it trade tokenized U.S. stocks without registering as an exchange, according to its public notice.

Trading would run 24 hours a day, seven days a week, with each stock paired against a stablecoin, including such as USDC and Tether's USDT Trades would go through automated liquidity pools on OKX's X Layer blockchain, built on Uniswap (UNI) v4. Only wallets holding a special access token issued by the venue would be able to trade, the notice said.

UNISWAP was one of the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. UNISWAP's price was up by 3% during the past 24 hours. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around UNI moved to 'bullish' from 'neutral,' while chatter around it stayed at 'normal' levels over the past day.

title: Should You Sell Your Stocks Right Now? Here's What a Century's Worth of History Suggests.
detail:
Should You Sell Your Stocks Right Now? Here's What a Century's Worth of History Suggests.
Jennifer Saibil, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 1, 2026 at 12:35 PM CST 5 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The forerunner of today's S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) goes back to 1926, when the S&P 90 was created as a stock market index. It was changed to 500 companies in 1957, and as of this year, there's a century's worth of data to inform investors about historical trends.

That small start 100 years ago preceded the worst stock market crash in U.S. history, but a century later, the index is thriving, even though it's had its ups and downs over the decades.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Is there eventually going to be another down? Most certainly. Should you sell your stocks beforehand? Like most things in life, it depends. Here's what you need to know.

The S&P 500 is at record levels

The S&P 500 is up 13% this year and hit its most recent record on Oct. 6. If it remains this way by the end of the year, it will be the fourth year in a row with double-digit gains.

Image source: Getty Images.

Many of those gains are due to the massive tech companies that anchor the index. It's weighted, which means that the largest stocks by market cap account for the most weight. Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet are its top five stocks by weight, and there isn't a non-artificial intelligence (AI) stock in the top 10. 39.7% of the index is concentrated in tech stocks, which means it's highly exposed to changes in AI and the tech sector.

Today's enthusiasm for AI stocks is to some degree propping up the rest of the market, but the economy as a whole has been robust despite inflation. Companies have been reporting strong growth, leading to confidence in their stocks. However, prices are outpacing growth, leading to an expensive market.

Should you sell before the fall?

There are signs that a crash could potentially happen soon. The CAPE ratio, which measures the average 10-year adjusted price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, is at its second-highest level ever at almost 41. When it reached a record of 44 in 2000, the market crashed. It didn't reach its previous high until seven years later.

The AI build-out is eerily reminiscent of the dot-com bubble at that time. While the S&P 500 is reaching highs, and with the prospect of a fall, you might be tempted to sell your stocks and pocket your gains. But that's a flawed argument.

First, no one knows when the crash is coming. There could be another year, or more, before it happens. If you sell now, you'll lose the chance to see your stocks continue to compound. Even if the market crashes, selling now means you miss the chance to see your stocks rebound and go even higher. As the saying goes, time in, not timing, the market is what matters.

So it's more than reasonable to expect a bear market this year or next, and to expect it to not last too long -- though it might.

Is your money parked in the right places?

The big question, then, is how you as an investor should deal with this situation.

My main piece of advice would be to have your money parked in the right places. And by that, I mean your short-term money -- funds that you expect to need within five years or so -- should not be in the stock market, as it's a volatile place. If there's a market crash and a bear market that lasts, say, three or more years, you don't want the accounts you planned to draw from to have temporarily shrunk. Short-term money can be stored in high-yield savings accounts, certificates of deposit (CDs), money market accounts, and bonds.

To be more conservative, you might keep money you'll need within 10 years in a less volatile place. And if you're approaching retirement, you might move a larger chunk of your portfolio out of stocks -- though remember that if you're, say, 60 and you might live for 25 more years, much of your nest egg will be remaining invested for many years, so keeping some of your portfolio in stocks should serve you well.

Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool

2026 hasn't been the best year for Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA). While it's up 13% versus 11% from the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC), Nvidia investors don't expect market-beating performance; they expect market-crushing performance. When you look at Nvidia's results, it's easy to see it should be doing better, as it grew revenue at 106% in the second quarter (Q2).

Over the long term, company growth and stock performance tend to be highly correlated, so what's up with the disconnect? I believe it's just the market lagging behind, and history tells us that right now is an incredible buying opportunity.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Nvidia is trading at a major discount

The best way to value Nvidia from a current and historical perspective is to utilize the forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio. This metric uses analysts' estimates for the full fiscal year to price the stock, so it bakes in some growth. At the start of a fiscal year, these measures tend to look pretty cheap, as there is a full year's worth of growth ahead. When you get halfway through the fiscal year (Q3 results aren't available yet), this starts to become a more conservative estimate, as only six months of growth are projected. So, sometimes stocks start to look a tad expensive toward the end of the year.

In both 2024 and 2025, Nvidia's stock reached 40 times forward earnings before the year was over. That's not the case this year.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts.

At just under 23 times forward earnings, Nvidia hasn't seen the end-of-year rally it normally does. This raises the question of why, and I think it's simply because the market is trying to call Nvidia's bluff (even if it's wrong). The S&P 500 trades at about 19.2 times forward earnings, so Nvidia trades at only a slight premium to the broader market. This is essentially the market conveying that after this year, it expects market-average growth from Nvidia.

But according to Nvidia and Wall Street analysts, that's a gross error. Nvidia itself told investors during its Q2 earnings call that it expects 70% revenue growth next year. It's rare for a company to provide next-year guidance six months before the year begins, but it shows the confidence Nvidia has in its future growth. This is likely because many of its clients have locked in orders for next year, giving it high visibility of what's to come. Wall Street analysts are also bullish, expecting 68% revenue growth next fiscal year.

All of this adds up to a company that will deliver excellent growth next year, which should result in huge returns.

Nvidia has major upside

If we value Nvidia's stock using next fiscal year's estimates, the stock trades for just 13.3 times earnings.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts.

So, if Nvidia hits all projections and the stock doubles, that means it would only trade for 26 times trailing earnings. That's a reasonable price tag for a company of Nvidia's stature and pedigree, so expecting the stock to rise significantly over the next year isn't out of the question. As a result, I think the historical record is pretty clear that the future is bright for Nvidia.

But that's just 2027. Beyond 2027, there's a broad expectation for the AI build-out to last through at least 2030, giving Nvidia even more time to capitalize on a generational growth opportunity. There are few better buys in the market than Nvidia right now, and investors shouldn't wait around too long; now is the time to strike.
